synthesis.headline: A maturing northern cyclone finally aims relief at the cornered southern heat dome — while the high-latitude ridge collapses and the West tips trough-dominant
synthesis.narrative:
The three-part meridional arrangement Tlaloc has tracked all week is still on the board, but the balance is tipping. The northern-stream system that ejected into Canada yesterday is now a mature 999-1000 mb low over the upper Great Lakes, trailing the day's tightest cold front southwestward through the central Plains and mid-Mississippi Valley — that corridor holds the strongest surface gradient and the most concentrated frontal lift. This is the front that will finally break the south-central heat late Wednesday. Aloft the pattern is a moderate-amplitude trough-ridge-trough: a broad longwave trough over the central U.S. with a weak closed low near Oklahoma/northern Texas, a ridge over the Intermountain West, and a second ridge over the Great Lakes and northeastern Canada. The southern Plains "cutoff" is worth a caveat — its innermost contour reads about 594 dam, a high value that marks a modest perturbation embedded in still-high heights rather than a deep, cold cutoff, so it does nothing to unseat the surface heat. Along the Gulf and Southeast a moist tropical airmass sits under a nearly isobar-free, slack gradient with a stalled boundary, leaving convection there to diurnal heating and low-level convergence.

Today's centers of action have quieted relative to yesterday. The severe threat has stepped down from yesterday's supercell/hail/tornado corridor to a wind-dominant SPC slight risk over central Iowa and far eastern Nebraska, where the cold front meets afternoon heating with 30-35 kt effective shear favoring line segments and damaging gusts; morning convection weakening and lingering inhibition cap the upside. Heavy rain is the co-threat on the front's cool side, with a slight excessive-rainfall risk in Iowa Wednesday and central Missouri into Thursday. The durable domestic signal remains the entrenched south-central heat — upper 90s to triple digits from the central Plains into the mid-Mississippi Valley through Wednesday with record warmth in play — before the front drops northern New England into the 30s Wednesday morning. In Canada, the interior British Columbia/Alberta ridge (a 1029 hPa center) sets up a firm gradient with a separate high to its south, while an active frontal system with 996-1000 mb lows works the BC/Pacific Northwest coast; the 988-992 hPa lows plotted far poleward are Arctic features, not a threat to the provinces. Over Mexico the North American Monsoon rolls on across the interior and Sierra Madre.

Aloft, the tightly packed contours and the sharp, cyclonically curved dry streamer curling from the upper Great Lakes into the Ohio Valley on the Air Mass RGB mark the jet corridor doing the work — that is the dynamical support behind the northern cyclone and its convection. The broad red-orange dry swath over the central and southern Plains is low-PV subsidence air under the late-summer ridge (its diffuse, warm-season character argues against a stratospheric intrusion), and midlevel warming, subsidence, and capping under it are why the heat holds, not any single surface high. The evolution question is whether the meridional regime is regenerating or genuinely transitioning, and the ensemble pair now leans toward transition. At 6-10 days the positive height anomaly sits over the Canadian Arctic while the Pacific Northwest and western Canada carry a well-below-normal trough and the ridge axis runs meridionally near 100-105W over the south-central U.S.; by 8-14 days that Arctic ridge has collapsed into a deep closed low, the positive anomalies have retreated to the southern U.S. and northern Mexico, and western Canada and the northern Rockies stay firmly trough-dominant. That is the ridge contracting geographically toward the southern tier — the classic retreat-toward-the-Southwest-while-the-north-cools signature — not the poleward regeneration read of yesterday. The WPC extended discussion supports this: a cold front sweeps the northern tier this weekend, a compact closed low drops into the Northwest and progresses into the northern Plains with moderate-to-heavy rain and northern Rockies wintry potential, another shortwave follows next Tuesday, and southern-tier ridging persists to keep the south-central heat and Four Corners monsoon going. Read together, the high-latitude/western amplification is fading toward a mobile, trough-dominant north and west, with the ridge surviving mainly as a heat anchor over the south.
synthesis.climate_context: ENSO is in a strong El Niño, with the ONI reaching roughly +1.80 for June-August 2026 after a steady, reversal-free warming trend out of last winter's weak La Niña. The tropics are behaving to type: a hyperactive East Pacific carries Hurricane Lowell near Kauai, Tropical Storm Marie west of Mexico, and a disturbance southwest of Mexico with a 70 percent chance of development this week (plus a lower-odds low south of Baja), set against a completely suppressed Atlantic where NHC expects no development for seven days — a textbook El Niño basin split arriving right at the climatological peak of the Atlantic season. The North American Monsoon remains active across the Southwest, Four Corners, and interior Mexico, and late-summer severe weather continues in its expected ridge-periphery and frontal mode across the northern Plains and Upper Midwest rather than as deep-Plains outbreaks. The most durable regional signal remains the south-central U.S. heat, which WPC expects to linger with Major-to-Extreme HeatRisk and record temperatures into next weekend as it contracts toward the southern Plains.
synthesis.regional_notes: SPC has no active mesoscale discussions. The immediate watch item is the wind-dominant severe risk in central Iowa and far eastern Nebraska this afternoon and evening as the cold front interacts with a destabilized airmass; terrain storms over central Colorado may move east into western Kansas at modest intensity. Flash-flood sensitivity runs with the slight excessive-rainfall risk in Iowa Wednesday and central Missouri into Thursday, plus a marginal Southwest flash-flood threat that may nudge into interior California. Note the sharp cold surge behind the front — 30s Wednesday morning in northern New England — and wintry potential in the northern Rockies this coming weekend. On the coasts, the BC/Pacific Northwest frontal system is the active Canadian feature, and monsoonal showers and storms continue over the Four Corners and interior Mexico.

sources.title: Surface Analysis
sources.summary: This 0900Z 8 September 2026 WPC surface analysis shows a sprawling high pressure regime dominating most of the central and eastern United States, with multiple modest centers in the 1018–1026 mb range that are individually unremarkable for early September. The most significant synoptic feature is a 999–1000 mb low centered over the upper Great Lakes region, trailing a cold front southwestward through the central Plains and a warm front extending eastward into the northeastern U.S.; the cold front shows the tightest isobar spacing on the chart, implying the strongest surface pressure gradient and wind field in the corridor from roughly the central Plains into the mid-Mississippi Valley, which is where frontal lift is most concentrated. A secondary low complex near the southern Rockies and New Mexico, with centers reading near 1007–1012 mb, anchors a diffuse frontal boundary extending southward through the Desert Southwest, though isobar spacing there is slack and the lift signal is weak. Across the Gulf Coast and southeastern states, the pattern is nearly isobar-free, indicating a very slack gradient; the combination of surface dewpoints reading into the upper 70s F in that region and the absence of organized lift suggests convection there would be driven primarily by diurnal heating and low-level moisture convergence rather than synoptic forcing. The 1086 mb value printed in the upper right corner appears likely to be a data or annotation artifact rather than a true pressure reading, as it would be extraordinary and no closed contours support it.

sources.title: Canadian Surface Analysis
sources.summary: This CMC surface analysis valid 0000Z Tuesday 09 August 2026 shows a broad high pressure ridge dominating much of central and western Canada, with the 1029 hPa center plotted over what appears to be the interior of British Columbia or Alberta and a separate 1029 hPa high centered well south of the border over the central United States, together establishing a strong pressure gradient across the northern Plains and Prairie provinces consistent with northerly flow aloft. A frontal boundary, marked with both warm and cold front symbols, extends from a low near the Pacific coast of the continent southward and then curves eastward, with the associated 996 and 1000 hPa lows sitting in the vicinity of the Pacific Northwest and southern British Columbia border region, suggesting active frontal lift along the BC coast. Over the Canadian interior, isobar spacing is relatively relaxed under the ridge, but to the northeast the chart shows a complex of lows in the 988 to 992 hPa range positioned well poleward, consistent with systems over the Arctic Ocean or Archipelago rather than the provinces, so those should not be read as threats to populated Canada. A low labeled 1012 hPa appears on the chart in a position that, relative to the Pacific coastline geometry visible here, could place it near or just off the Alaskan Panhandle or northern BC coast, with a frontal tail extending southward and connecting to the coastal baroclinic zone. The eastern Canadian domain, from roughly Ontario eastward to the Maritimes, appears to sit under a broad but weakening ridge, with no sharp frontal boundaries evident over that region at this analysis time.

sources.title: 500 mb Analysis
sources.summary: At 1200 UTC 8 September 2026, the 500 mb pattern shows a broad longwave trough across the central United States with a closed low centered over the southern Plains near Oklahoma or northern Texas, where the innermost contour reads approximately 594 dam — a notably high value for a closed low in that position, suggesting only a modest depression rather than a deep cutoff, though the closed circulation is clearly depicted and implies the system is at least temporarily self-retaining rather than translating rapidly downstream. To the west, a ridge axis extends from the Pacific coast high pressure area across the Intermountain West, and to the northeast a second strong ridge is evident over the upper Great Lakes and northeastern Canada, where heights approach 588-594 dam; this eastern ridge and the central trough form a moderate-amplitude longwave pattern, but there is no clear high-over-low stacking at the same longitude that would constitute a Rex block. Two green-shaded regions, which by convention on College of DuPage charts indicate 500 mb temperature departures, mark unseasonably cool air over the central Rockies into the central Plains and a separate area over the upper Midwest and Great Lakes, consistent with the troughing aloft. The flow appears relatively progressive across the northern tier, with tightly packed contours over the upper Midwest implying an implied jet corridor there, while the closed low over the southern Plains anchors a more stagnant, negatively tilted short-wave feature in that sector. No strongly amplified blocking geometry is present; rather, this is a moderate-amplitude trough-ridge-trough pattern with the southern Plains cutoff as the most dynamically noteworthy feature.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB (GOES-19)
sources.summary: This GOES-19 Air Mass RGB from 1331Z on 08 September 2026 shows a broad swath of orange-red tones across the central and southern Plains into the mid-Mississippi Valley, consistent with dry upper-tropospheric air under what is likely a broad upper-level ridge, not a stratospheric intrusion given the diffuse, warm-season character of the signal. A more compact and sharper dry streamer extends southward from the upper Great Lakes region into the Ohio Valley, curling around the eastern flank of a trough whose cloud signature is visible as the white-gray convective mass over the Great Lakes and upper Midwest; that boundary between the dry orange airmass and the green moist air to its east marks the implied jet corridor. Scattered deep convective cells, appearing as bright white tops, are visible across the Gulf of Mexico and into southern Florida and the western Caribbean, embedded in broadly green tropical moisture. Along the mid-Atlantic and New England coastline a thin arc of cirrus-topped cloud is present on the immediate western edge of the maritime green airmass, consistent with outflow or a frontal boundary trailing from the northern cyclone. The southwestern corner of the domain shows a separate pocket of orange-red dry air over Baja California and the adjacent Pacific, unrelated to the central U.S. pattern.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB Full Disk (GOES-19)
sources.summary: The most prominent airmass boundary on this image runs across southern Canada and the northeastern United States, where a sharp color transition from blue-purple in the north to green southward marks the polar front and the implied jet corridor at upper levels. A well-organized cyclonic system is visible in the upper right of the disk near Atlantic Canada and the northwestern Atlantic, with a tight white cloud head and trailing cloud band consistent with a mature extratropical cyclone. In the tropics, scattered clusters of bright white deep convective tops are present over southern Mexico, Central America, and the western Caribbean, with additional convective activity visible over the Amazon basin, though no single cluster shows the tight circular organization that would suggest a developing tropical cyclone. The broad green tones dominating the tropics from the eastern Pacific through equatorial South America indicate a deep, moist tropical airmass, while the orange-red colors over the southern United States and northern Mexico reflect dry, subsident upper-tropospheric air under what is consistent with a late-summer ridge rather than a stratospheric intrusion. Southern South America and the South Atlantic show active baroclinic features rendered in blue-purple and white, indicating cold polar air masses and frontal cloud bands well south of 40S.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day Temperature Outlook
sources.summary: The most striking feature is the high-confidence above-normal signal across the Southeast, Gulf Coast, and Texas, where the darkest red shading indicates a 90-100% probability of above-normal temperatures for September 13-17, 2026. That signal weakens but remains likely (60-80%) across the central and southern Plains, the mid-Atlantic, and into the Carolinas, while a separate above-normal signal at the 80-90% level covers most of Alaska. Contrasting sharply, a below-normal signal arches across the northern tier from the northern Rockies through the northern Plains and into the Upper Midwest, reaching 60-70% probability at its core over the Dakotas and Minnesota region, with the Pacific Coast and portions of the interior West holding near-normal odds. The sharp latitudinal gradient between the below-normal north and above-normal south, concentrated in the central part of the country, is consistent with a persistent amplified upper-level ridge positioned over the southern and eastern US and a downstream or upstream trough anchored over the northern Rockies and High Plains — implying the CPC sees little evidence of pattern breakdown at this range. New England and the immediate Northeast coast are largely near-normal, suggesting the ridge axis does not extend cleanly into that region, or that sufficient spread exists there to prevent a confident warm signal.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This is the CPC 6-10 day 500 mb height and height-anomaly forecast valid 13-17 September 2026, with heights in dam (solid green, 60 m interval) and anomalies in dashed contours (blue negative, red positive).

The dominant positive anomaly center sits over the Canadian Arctic Archipelago and northern Baffin Island region, labeled near +90 dam on the chart — but that reading almost certainly reflects meters rather than decameters, placing the actual positive departure at roughly +9 dam, which is a strong but plausible ridge anomaly for an ensemble mean. A secondary positive center appears over the north-central Pacific. The most prominent negative anomaly center is over western Canada and the U.S. Pacific Northwest, with blue dashed contours suggesting values around -90 to -150 on the plotted scale, again most plausibly interpreted as roughly -9 to -15 dam in true anomaly units, indicating a well-below-normal trough anchored over that region.

The 500 mb height ridge axis, inferred from the packing and curvature of the solid green contours, runs roughly meridionally near 100-105°W from the central U.S. southward, with heights reaching 588 dam across the south-central U.S. and northern Mexico. A trough axis is implied over the Pacific Northwest and British Columbia, where contours show strong cyclonic curvature and the negative anomalies are concentrated. The zero anomaly line appears to cut through the interior of the continent well east of the Rockies, meaning positive anomalies over the western ridge have retreated substantially eastward; the western U.S. sits under negative departures, suggesting the amplified western ridge has collapsed and the pattern is trending toward a more mobile, trough-dominant western regime rather than a persistently amplified western ridge.

sources.title: CPC 8-14 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary: This chart is a 500 mb geopotential height and height anomaly (departures from normal, dashed contours) prognostic valid 15–21 September 2026, made 7 September 2026 — consistent with a CPC 8–14 day product. The dominant feature is a deep closed low centered over the Canadian Arctic Archipelago, with the innermost contour reading approximately 528 dam; the implied anomaly pattern around this low is strongly negative, consistent with a large negative height anomaly of order +10 or more dam below normal across the central to eastern Canadian Arctic. Downstream, the 500 mb height contours over the contiguous United States tighten from roughly 564 dam across the northern Rockies and northern Plains to 588–594 dam across the southern Plains and Gulf Coast, with no closed ridge or positive anomaly center apparent over western Canada, the northern Rockies, or the northern Plains — the ridge axis, where contours are most amplified, appears to sit well to the south and east, roughly over the central to southern United States, not over the northern tier. The dashed anomaly contours (red positive, blue negative) show a negative anomaly region extending from the Arctic low southward into central Canada, while positive anomaly values appear concentrated across the southern United States and northern Mexico, indicating the ridge core has retreated well southward relative to normal. Western Canada and the northern Rockies fall clearly within the negative or near-neutral anomaly zone, making this a trough-dominated, below-normal height pattern for those regions during the valid period.

sources.title: WPC Short Range Forecast Discussion
sources.summary: A frontal system trailing from an intensifying low over southern Canada is driving strong to severe thunderstorms and heavy rainfall across the upper Midwest and central Plains early Tuesday, shifting southeastward through Wednesday into interior New England. WPC highlights slight risk of excessive rainfall across Iowa Wednesday and central Missouri into Thursday. A stalled frontal boundary across the eastern Gulf Coast and Florida will maintain scattered showers and thunderstorms through the period. Dangerous heat persists from central Plains to mid-Mississippi Valley through Wednesday with upper-90s to triple-digit temperatures before relief arrives late Wednesday. Northern New England will see cold air surge with temperatures dropping to 30s Wednesday morning. Marginal flash flood risk continues across Southwest through Wednesday, possibly extending into interior California.

sources.title: SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook
sources.summary:
Slight risk of severe thunderstorms over central Iowa and far eastern Nebraska Tuesday afternoon/evening, mainly from severe wind gusts. More sporadic severe wind and large hail possible across upper Midwest into central Plains.

An extensive low-level jet supports warm-air advection and ongoing convection from eastern Nebraska through Wisconsin. Morning activity will gradually weaken and shift northeast, limiting destabilization. Moderate buoyancy possible in Minnesota ahead of an eastward-moving cold front, but lingering convective inhibition and considerable uncertainty preclude severe probabilities. South and west from Iowa through eastern Nebraska, strong daytime heating will create moderate to strong instability by late afternoon. Storm development expected as the cold front interacts with this air mass. Effective bulk shear of 30-35 knots supports organization into line segments with some damaging wind gusts likely. Low tornado risk expected but outflow-dominant storms will limit tornadoes. Central Colorado terrain storms likely with modest intensity possible as they move eastward into western Kansas.

sources.title: SPC Mesoscale Discussions
sources.summary: No mesoscale discussions active. SPC is not tracking any organized convective threat requiring immediate monitoring at this time.

sources.title: NHC Tropical Weather Outlooks
sources.summary:
Atlantic: No tropical cyclone formation expected over the next 7 days across the Atlantic, Caribbean, or Gulf of America.

East Pacific: Hurricane Lowell near Kauai and Tropical Storm Marie west of Mexico currently active. A broad low pressure area southwest of Mexico shows organizing convection with gradual development likely; tropical depression expected to form later this week while moving west-northwest at 10-15 mph (70 percent 7-day formation chance). A second low several hundred miles south of Baja California's tip may develop this weekend or early next week with lower development potential (20 percent 7-day chance).

sources.title: ENSO State (Oceanic Niño Index)
sources.summary: ONI shows weak La Niña conditions currently (NDJ 2025 at -0.60). The anomaly is moderating through early 2026, crossing into slightly warm territory by February-March. By mid-2026, anomalies strengthen substantially, with the index reaching +1.80 by June-August 2026, indicating a transition toward El Niño. Warming trend accelerates notably from spring onward.

sources.title: Teleconnection Indices (PNA, AO, NAO)
sources.summary: PNA is weakly negative (latest -0.34, 7-day mean -0.58) with little recent trend, suggesting marginal support for eastern troughing. AO flipped positive today (+0.53) after several days negative, leaving the 7-day mean near zero—high-latitude blocking signal is mixed. NAO has fallen notably to -1.01 (7-day mean), a 0.49 unit drop from the prior week, now solidly negative; this favors Atlantic blocking and may influence whether cutoff lows escape. These are summer values, so treat as directional guidance rather than canonical signals.
